tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (bench/parser_bench.ml orchestrating bench/parser_ocaml_bench.ml and bench/cpp/parser_cpp_bench.cpp, which runs RapidJSON/nlohmann/sajson/simdjson under Google Benchmark), and the snapshot page states compilers (OxCaml 5.2.0+ox, GCC 15.2.1), flags (OCaml perf profile -g/-gdwarf flags, C++ CMake Release) and CPU (i7-12700K, pinned P-core). All A criteria met.

corrections.claimed_speedup: simdjson-ox-tape-reusable (reusable tape parser) geomean 1247.7 MB/s vs rapidjson-dom 1059.7 MB/s (~1.18x, derived from page data; README states 118% of RapidJSON) and vs nlohmann-json-dom 132.2 MB/s (~9.4x, derived from page data). Per fixture the tape-reusable mode beats RapidJSON on apache_builds (1555 vs 867 MB/s), citm_catalog (2072 vs 1649), gsoc-2018 (2257 vs 1092) and twitter (1428 vs 1048) but is slower on canada (759 vs 990), marine_ik (668 vs 885) and numbers (894 vs 1047). The recommended DOM API is slower than RapidJSON: simdjson-ox-reusable 729.5 MB/s and one-shot simdjson-ox 659.4 MB/s geomean (README: 69% of RapidJSON). Still behind C++ simdjson-dom (3344.5 MB/s) and sajson-dom (1650.9 MB/s).
corrections.caveats: The win over RapidJSON comes only from the lower-level tape mode with a reusable parser (zero OCaml allocation in the loop), while the RapidJSON harness builds a fresh rapidjson::Document every iteration. The author says tape vs DOM APIs 'are not identical enough for a strictly like-for-like comparison'. The recommended DOM API is about 0.69x RapidJSON, and tape mode loses to RapidJSON on 3 of 7 fixtures (canada, marine_ik, numbers). The author labels it a single-run, point-in-time snapshot (turbo on, frequency not locked). x86-only SIMD. Very new project with 3 stars.

notes: Every number in the record matches the 2026-08-15 snapshot table and geomean ranking. Metadata checked via gh: MIT, 3 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-08-23. The claim is accurate for the named tape-reusable variant, but the headline 'faster than RapidJSON' does not hold for the library's default DOM API. Corrections make that explicit.

tier_reason: The README states ratios against Json.NET and others, and they trace to a 2014 single-blog benchmark (theburningmonk, SimpleSpeedTester harness) with results only as images. It gives no CPU, .NET runtime or build flags, and it is not a well-known benchmark suite, so tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README states 3.4x faster than JSON.NET, 2.4x than ServiceStack JSON, 1.8x than Jil, 6x than JSON.NET BSON, 16.5x than JavaScriptSerializer, 4.3x than DataContractJsonSerializer, 1.6x than protobuf-net. In the linked 2014 theburningmonk results table (image), these ratios match serialization times only: NetJson 112.24 ms vs Json.Net 380.59 ms (~3.39x, derived from linked table data). Deserialization gain is smaller: 175.00 ms vs 437.53 ms (~2.5x vs Json.NET, derived). In that same table protobuf-net beat NetJSON on both serialization (100.68 vs 112.24 ms) and deserialization (163.20 vs 175.00 ms). The README's 1.6x-vs-protobuf-net figure comes from its own separate log: serialization 157.99 vs 257.98 ms, deserialization about equal (252.18 vs 251.50 ms).
corrections.workload: Serialization and deserialization of a simple object (SimpleSpeedTester harness, theburningmonk 2014 JSON serializers benchmark), comparing NetJSON with Json.NET 6.0.4, ServiceStack.Text 4.0.24, Jil 1.7.0, protobuf-net, JavaScriptSerializer, DataContractJsonSerializer and others. The README's headline ratios correspond to serialization times.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 238 stars; NuGet package NetJSON (latest 1.4.7, ~1.22M total downloads)
corrections.caveats: The README ratios are serialization-only figures from a 2014 third-party blog post whose results are images, with no CPU, .NET runtime version or build configuration disclosed. The deserialization advantage is smaller (~2.5x vs Json.NET). The cited blog table shows protobuf-net faster than NetJSON, contradicting the README's 1.6x claim, which comes from a separate undocumented run. Library versions are over a decade old. The blog's 'System.Text.Json 1.9.9.1' is an unrelated old package, and Microsoft's modern System.Text.Json incumbent was not tested.

notes: Downgraded for an overstated claim, not tier: the record presented serialization-only ratios as a round-trip result, and the cited source contradicts the protobuf-net ratio. The earlier caveat that the ratios could not be checked is wrong: the blog's second image is a readable ms table that matches the README's serialization ratios. Metadata checked: MIT, 238 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-05 (active).

tier_reason: First-party README table produced by public benchmark code (benchmark/benchmark.js, Benchmark.js suite of simdjson.lazyParse vs JSON.parse). The page gives no compiler or Node.js version, and the CPU is only '2018 MacBook Pro, 2.3GHz Intel Core i9' without a model, so not A. It is not third-party, so not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Page 'X faster' column (simdjson.lazyParse vs JSON.parse) ranges from 0.77x to 2.30x and is faster on 11 of 15 files. Examples: sf_citylots.json 1492.166 ms vs 709.692 ms = 2.10x (stated on page); numbers.json 2.30x. Slower on citm_catalog.json (0.93x), random.json (0.78x) and twitter.json (0.77x). About even on update_center (1.03x) and instruments (1.09x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the benchmark page; binding.gyp builds the addon in Release config with -O3 -std=c++17 (node-addon-api). Compiler and Node.js versions unstated.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 620 stars; npm package "simdjson" (latest 0.9.2, ~45.9k downloads in the month ending 2026-09-21)
corrections.caveats: The comparison is not like-for-like: lazyParse returns an external C++ parsed-document handle without building JS objects, while JSON.parse builds the full JS object graph. The README and issue #5 note that the eager simdjson.parse, which converts to JS objects, is much slower. Hardware is a 2018 laptop, with no compiler or Node version given. Not uniformly faster: slower on 3 of 15 corpus files. Unmaintained since Feb 2023 (>3 years). Vendors an old simdjson.

notes: The numbers match the README table exactly, including the lower bound. The record left out that random.json (0.78x) was also slower. Metadata checked via gh: Apache-2.0, 620 stars, not archived or forked, last commit 2023-02-23, so 'abandoned' is correct. The main speed comes from wrapping C++ simdjson (a seed/known project), but this is a distinct binding project with its own benchmark.
